defenses.response: Reading the reviewer's own sentence closely: 'The authors should discuss how the derived TRACE PENALTY AND DESIGN-IMBALANCE TERMS are expected to behave under non-normal likelihoods, and whether THE CURRENT FINDINGS can be safely generalized to standard GLM frameworks used in applied research.' The antecedent of 'the current findings' in this sentence is the two items just named a few words earlier -- the trace penalty and the design-imbalance terms -- not an unbounded reference to every identity the paper derives. Neither of those two named quantities IS the known-scale collapse. The trace penalty is the +1/2 tr(RIV) general-case headline; the design-imbalance terms are the (A)+(C) MAR/MCAR mechanism terms; the known-scale collapse is a third, separate boundary result the paper itself frames as a scope LIMIT on the theorem (G6, S4-P8), not as one of the applied 'findings' used anywhere in the paper's own applications. A reviewer asking whether findings used in applied research (AIC/BIC/LRT correction) generalize to GLMs is asking about exactly the quantities named in their own sentence, which is the general/estimated-scale case Gamma and (after correction) Bernoulli both test. I do not think 'the current findings' plausibly stretches to include a boundary identity the reviewer never mentions and the paper itself does not use in any application.
defenses.amendment: Add the scope-limiting sentence already promised (Discussion G9 and response-letter r3#2) not as a hedge against an ambiguous reading, but as a stated interpretive choice: 'This illustration addresses the trace penalty and design-imbalance terms named in the reviewer's own question -- the quantities the paper's applications actually use. The known-scale collapse is a separate boundary result, not used in any application, and remains verified only in the multivariate normal family (G6); closing that gap is a distinct question this illustration does not address.' This makes the reading an explicit, defensible editorial choice rather than a silent omission, and invites the reviewer to say so if they intended the broader reading.
defenses.residual_risk: A reviewer who did mean the broader reading could still ask for the known-scale case explicitly in a second round; the stated interpretive choice makes that a normal, answerable follow-up rather than evidence of an evaded question. I am reluctant to concede this point outright because the textual reading is genuinely the more natural one, but I acknowledge it is a reading, not a certainty, and the disclosure is what keeps that honest.
